decisions.reason: VMW §2.3.1 assigns current operations to the control state; scanned symbols and the current measurement outcome select the next state and moves. Corrected this source-fidelity defect without changing operation families or resource accounting.

The range-OR loop ran its body on an initially empty interval: M=4,l=r=1 starts L=R=5 and selects spurious nodes. A pre-tested L<R loop with zero accumulator returns zero immediately and partitions every nonempty interval into disjoint tree nodes. The statement is unchanged.

The binary-output definition of time-constructibility itself supplies an O(R) constructor. Run it on virtual unary input by mapping each nonblank input symbol to 1, without copying or scanning all n symbols. A binary countdown streams R choices in O(R) total time (amortized bit carries), so the explicit selector/padding construction works even for bounded sublinear clocks. Its count (2^(R+2)-1)A proves both strict sides and complement correctly; the source page’s at-least-linear clock convention is unnecessary for this explicit construction.

If the start state halts and there are no nonhalting states, a valid empty transition table need not bound binary-encoded tape/head counts by polynomial description length. The original per-head initialization could violate the claimed time bound. Validation now counts actual fields, treats zero expected rows without exponent expansion, and returns the initial outcome before allocating per-head data. Nonhalting starts still force an explicit row, proving all parameter bounds.

F1 explicitly cites the supplier's construction. Its proof 2.2 charges total fresh word lengths; 2.3 defines a=PB+r; 3.2 registers neighboring blocks; 4.3 proves the three-block cache invariant; 6.4 and 7.2 implement short physical pointers with fixed heads. The consumer replaces only the dictionaries, proves AVL/rank/OR operations locally, and inherits the early return for initially halting sources. These are actual proved prerequisites, not missing assumptions.

The consumer explicitly justifies exact relativization at 4.1. Fixing an exact oracle makes each R-bit random string determine one outcome, so the identical selector construction has acceptance (1-2^(-R-2))A/2^R, with unchanged oracle calls and O(R) additional deterministic/fair-bit work. Its complement therefore works for MAJ and AND; no probabilistic-oracle closure is asserted. Checkpoint tuples have qS=O(n), bottom native-query tests cost O(S+n), and fixed circuit depth yields a fixed hierarchy level.

The actual normalized interpreter explicitly emits only padded q-bit physical pointers (clocked simulation 7.2), and basis normalization 6.2 and 7.1 use only those short work/input indices. With fixed description and n<=T, q=O(log T). Long padded source indices are saved arrays, not physical emitted indices. Thus the Cook trace correctly stores short accumulator values/lengths; sorting enforces memory consistency and deterministic gate clauses give the unique witness.

F4 explicitly selects the prefix-free code, and the clocked-simulation proof 1.1 constructs unary block counts and unary-length binary tuple fields with profile/table delimiters. These parse in polynomial code length by 2.1, independently of the generic effective encoding. Every fixed code eventually fits c0 log n, while a<a'<b absorbs the interpreter overhead. Source-clock tie normalization and complementation give the stated diagonal contradiction.

A four-element subset cannot itself be dense in SU(2). The corrected statement asserts density of its generated subgroup, exactly as proved in 2.1 and required by the gate-package definition. The monic-polynomial argument proves irrationality, the two axes generate SU(2) after closure, and the finite mesh plus certified word search proves the stated base net. Gate entries and the phase-erasure map are unchanged.

The separate theorem thm-qc-basic-rewrite-correct-and-terminating already proves all cancellations from the exact H,T,T-dagger,CNOT matrices and proves termination by strict word-length decrease. Its second step also proves that the no-match stopping test returns a locally irreducible word. The algorithm gives exact inputs, rules, ordered supports, deterministic scan/restart and output; its output specification is justified by that separate result.

The actual supplier proof 3.1 states and applies central controlled-Z absorption, saving (4^(n-2)-1)/3 CNOTs; 4.1 applies terminal diagonal migration, saving 4^(n-2)-1 more. Subtracting from the unoptimized count yields the exact displayed 23/48 formula. The supplier separately treats n=1 and n=0. A1 accurately describes its full proved construction, so the corollary imports no unsupported optimization.

The full multicontrol supplier proof 1.1 and 2.1 constructs unitary square roots and the no-workspace recursion. The one-control supplier proof 1.1 gives the exact A,B,C Euler/half-angle formulas and 3.1 retains the control phase; the Gray-path algorithm also spells out those expansions. The consumer independently constructs effective roots via separated eigenvalues and projectors, hardcoding finitely many branch decisions and positive divisor bounds. Its phase-root formulas avoid computing arguments and preserve polynomial Cauchy time for the fixed finite family.

The QSD corollary explicitly imports the exact QC11 construction. Its underlying supplier proof 2.1 sets c2=3, 3.1 counts zero nonterminal savings at n=2, and 4.1 states N=1 so no diagonal migration occurs. A1 accurately describes this actual proof. Substitution gives 23/3-6+4/3=3, a CNOT construction count only.

The original title omitted the derived-basis access restriction and suggested an unqualified PTISP simulation. Renamed it to BQTISP to Derived-Basis PrTISP Simulation, preserving the complete Statement. Also corrected proof 3.1’s numerator cross-reference from 2.1 to 2.2. Reviewed fixed-factor compilation, orthogonal measurement-history rephasing, signed path pairs, exact native queries on separate rows, and fixed-length choice counting; all preserve the stated basis-profile time and operand extent.
